We did learn that this great victory in the Drugwar was the result of an 18-month-long investigation led by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, with the collaboration of narks in the Vancouver police.

Datillo alleged that U.S. undercover agents bought more than $12,000 US worth of marijuana seeds since March last year, including mail orders from nine states for more than $7,000 US worth of seeds.

During the past year, U.S. undercover agents also bought large quantities of seeds in person from the Hastings Street store four times and were given advice on how to smuggle them back into the U.S., Datillo said.

In addition to the evidence compiled by U.S. investigators, Datillo claimed that authorities have lined up eight former marijuana growers in the U.S. who will testify they bought seeds through Marc Emery Direct, or to anything else that they are forced to say.
(MarijuanaNews note: Someone who claims to have been a seed-grower for Marc is narking.)

At one point in the investigation, U.S. undercover agents even offered Emery $18,000 for 10 pounds of marijuana, but he referred them to a third party, which Emery's lawyer John Conroy said was proof that Emery dealt strictly in marijuana seeds.

Conroy said Emery had been operating his business since 1995 with the "passive acquiescence" of local law enforcement agencies and claimed he clearly posed no harm to the public if released.

While Datillo alleged the seed-selling business was a multi-million dollar operation, Conroy said that Emery, who rents a Vancouver apartment for $3,000 a month, had only $13 in his bank accounts and could not provide a large bail amount.
(MarijuanaNews note: Marc really is broke.)

"I think that while lots of money may have gone through the accounts, it didn't stay there," Conroy said after the hearing, suggesting most of Emery's business revenue was used to pay for political activism, including Pot-TV and Cannabis Culture magazine.

As a spokesperson for the BC Marijuana Party said, "There are dozens of seed sellers in Vancouver, there are seed sellers in the U.S., and you don't see them being targeted."

Excerpted from San Jose Mercury News: Mexico Now Dominates U.S.  Drug Distribution

DEA: Colombia Is No Longer No.  1 In $400 Billion Annual Trade

WASHINGTON - Mexican drug traffickers have pushed aside their Colombian counterparts and now dominate the U.S.  market in the biggest reorganization of the trade since the rise of the Colombian cartels in the 1980s, U.S.  officials say.

Mexican groups now are behind much of the cocaine, heroin, marijuana and methamphetamine on U.S.  streets, the officials say, with Mexican law enforcement agencies viewed as either too weak or too corrupt to stop them.

Mexico's role as a drug-trafficking hub has been growing for some time, but its grip on the $400 billion-a-year trade has strengthened in recent years.  According to the U.S.  Drug Enforcement Administration in June, 92 percent of the cocaine sold in the United States in 2004 came through the U.S.-Mexico border, compared with 77 percent in 2003.

Mexican drug rings offer a more varied menu of drugs than their Colombian counterparts, who traditionally dealt in cocaine and heroin.  According to the DEA, Mexico is the second-largest supplier of heroin in the United States after Colombia, and the largest foreign supplier of marijuana.
(MarijuanaNews note: Afghanistan has become the largest producer of opium for heroin, under the US occupation. Ironically, the UK is nominally in charge of much of the heroin producing area and most of Afghan heroin ends up in Europe.)

Excerpted from the San Antonio Express-News:
The U.S.  government is temporarily shutting its consulate in Nuevo Laredo, citing new safety concerns in the wake of a high-stakes drug-cartel turf war that intensified this week to include rocket-propelled grenades, officials said.

U.S.  Ambassador Tony Garza said an early Friday morning gangland battle involving "unusually advanced weaponry," led to the decision to close the consulate for all but emergency services for one week.

In the latest round of violence, two residential homes were targeted late Thursday and early Friday.  Both were sprayed with machine gun fire and one hit with what was believed to be grenade launcher.  According to media reports, more than 1,000 rounds were fired in the attack Thursday and at least three people may have been kidnapped.

The Associated Press reported from Nuevo Laredo:  "The battle left a residential street resembling a war zone. Grenades were strewn about the scene, and soldiers who moved in to recover them said they had been lobbed at the home and exploded."

Mexico's attorney general's office released a statement saying it is investigating the shooting and provided a detailed list of some of the items seized from an attacked home, including 14 photos of men in municipal police uniforms.

Printed in the Washington Post, the Miami Herald and other papers:

DRUG CZAR: MEDICAL POT USE 'DYING'

HONOLULU -- The White House drug czar said Friday that medical marijuana is "dying out" after the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that federal authorities may prosecute sick people whose doctors prescribe pot to ease pain.

John Walters, the national drug policy director, said state legislative efforts to expand medical marijuana programs have stalled in the two months since the high court's ruling overrode laws in Hawaii and nine other states.

"I think it's dying out," Walters told reporters after a meeting with Hawaii drug treatment counselors and law enforcement officials.  "The real issue here is, is it the safe and best way for medical treatment? We don't think the best thing for people who are really sick is to make them high and send them away."

Walters said the federal government was funding research into whether cannabis could be used as a source of "medically sound" drugs, but he said "smoked marijuana hasn't met that science."
